question: Can I accept food or masjid donations from someone whose income comes from selling alcohol?
answer:
The final point: the one whose income is derived from this, and it is a necessity, is forgiven. But the one whose income is derived from this, and it is not a necessity... And this is a common question: "My friend owns a store that sells alcohol; can I go eat at his house?" "My cousin, my brother-in-law owns a haram store, and he's invited me for dinner." Or in the masjid, the board committee: somebody might be very rich, but they own maybe sharab stores, and he writes a check of $50,000 to the masjid.

Actually, it would happen in the previous cities I was at that, astaghfirullah, astaghfirullah, some of our own brethren, they run liquor stores. I don't know if you are aware of this or not, but across this country there is a stereotype, which is partially true, of some of our Muslim brethren making an easy buck in particular neighborhoods of the city by opening liquor stores. And they get rich, because people are going to buy liquor, and they want to give to the masjid, and they give big checks to the masjid. And the same goes: can we go to their house, or whatnot?

And the response to this is as follows. That money technically is haram, and the more haram involved, the more haram the money is. If the guy owns a liquor store, this is much more haram than if he owns a generic restaurant that has liquor on the menu, which is more haram than if he owns a gas station, which has lots of halal things, and the majority of the income is from the gas and whatnot, and he has one beer that's being sold as well. So there are levels.

Now, technically speaking, **transferring of ownership transfers the hukm.** Meaning, if you own a store and somebody walks in, do you have to quiz the person when he buys, "Where did you get that money from?" When the ownership is transferred, the hukm is transferred. So from a purely fiqhi perspective, technically speaking, it is halal for anyone to engage with the money after the person has taken it.

But there's something else. It is called adab. It is called taqwa. Should you engage with this person's money? And this is a case-by-case basis. If it's your brother-in-law, your cousin, he owns a liquor store, you should send the message: "I don't want to eat at your house." Even if technically it might be halal, you need to send the message: "I'm not happy at what you're doing. You own a liquor store; how can I go and eat at your house?" There's adab and there's fatwa. Fiqh is one thing.

Technically speaking, the haram is between him and Allah. When he comes to you and he wants to purchase your car, he writes you a check: it's not your business where he got the money from. That check is halal for you to take. And the same goes if he gives you something: technically it is halal. But should you? That's now a case-by-case basis. And if you choose to do that, you will not be sinful. And if you choose to send the message, "I'm not happy," you will be rewarded. It's a matter of taqwa, that you are being extra strict and pious. And there is no question that this is a level of ihsan and taqwa, that you should avoid money that is haram, even if it's not haram for you. You get my point here: you know this money is haram.

Now, as for the masajid, the fatawa has come from many, many ulama and bodies that when somebody like this gives donations, we should not use that money for the musalla area, but we may use it for the parking lot, we may use it for reconstruction in the toilets. But the musalla area itself, it has a level of sanctity that we don't want to even corrupt. Even if technically the money is halal, we should try our best to not use that money for something that is so sacred.

And actually our scholars of fiqh mentioned this: if somebody gives haram money for the publication of mushafs, it should not be done, even though technically it might be halal, because you want to protect the mushaf. For the construction of the actual masjid, we say no, do something else; not the actual musalla where the salah takes place. And this again is not a fatwa of fiqh as much as it is adab of taqwa and of respecting the signs of Allah.
